1. Overview & Architectural Motivation

Retiam's core vector rendering engine provides foundational 2D primitives ([`Circle`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/src/engine/entities/primitives/2d/Circle.ts), `Rectangle`, [`Triangle`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/src/engine/entities/primitives/2d/Triangle.ts), [`Path`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/src/engine/entities/primitives/2d/Path.ts)) and basic 3D solids (`Box3D`, `Sphere3D`, `Cylinder3D`, `Cone3D`).

However, mathematical visualization, scientific illustration, infographic animation, and engineering pedagogy demand a dedicated, high-order geometry library capable of generating rich 2D vector curves ($C^1$ continuous Béziers, filleted $N$-gons, compound topology cutouts, involute gear teeth) and procedural 3D WebGPU meshes (Platonic solids with planar normals, swept curve parallel transport tubes, torus knots, and conical frustums).

To satisfy these requirements without bloating the core runtime, Retiam provides a dedicated library: **`retiam/shapes`** (located at [`libs/shapes/`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes)).
Core Principles

items: **Zero AI-Slop & Strict Mathematical Rigor**: All shapes are mathematically derived from exact closed-form equations (e.g., Lamé superellipses, Archimedean spirals, Frenet-Serret/Bishop parallel transport frames, and $C^1$ cubic Bézier splines).

**Native WebGPU Integration**: 2D shapes compile directly to SVG path data consumed by Retiam's Loop-Blinn analytical quadratic shader (`PathGeometry`) or CPU triangulator (`TriangulatedPathGeometry`). 3D shapes construct explicit vertex/normal/UV buffers (`WebGPUMesh`) rendered with Retiam's Cook-Torrance PBR shading.

**Planar Face Normals on Polyhedra**: Eliminates Phong/Gouraud curved specular distortion and perimeter edge banding on flat polyhedral faces (Platonic solids, prisms, wedges, pyramids) by generating distinct vertices per face with true planar normals.

**Dynamic Mutation & Invalidation**: Every shape features reactive getters and setters for its geometric parameters (e.g. `points`, `radius`, `teeth`, `cornerRadius`), automatically re-tessellating buffers and invalidating the scene graph.

blocks.text: 3. Mathematical Foundations: 2D Vector Curves
3.1. Corner Filleting with Interior Angle Bisectors

Sharp polygonal corners in [`Star`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/2d/Star.ts), [`RegularPolygon`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/2d/RegularPolygon.ts), [`Cross`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/2d/Cross.ts), and [`Chevron`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/2d/Chevron.ts) are filleted into smooth circular tangent arcs using closed-form interior bisector trigonometry:
Given three consecutive polygon vertices $P_{i-1}, P_i, P_{i+1}$, let the incoming and outgoing normalized edge vectors be:

The interior angle $\theta$ at vertex $P_i$ satisfies $\cos\theta = \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}$. The distance $d$ from the sharp corner $P_i$ to the tangent contact points $T_1$ and $T_2$ for a fillet radius $r$ is:
To prevent adjacent fillets from overlapping when edge length $L = \|P_{i+1} - P_i\|$ is short, the fillet radius is dynamically clamped:

The tangent entry point $T_1 = P_i + d \cdot \mathbf{u}$ connects to tangent exit point $T_2 = P_i + d \cdot \mathbf{v}$ via an exact circular arc of radius $r_{\text{clamped}}$ encoded into SVG path data using the `A` (elliptical arc) operator.
3.2. $C^1$ Continuous Cubic Bézier Curves (Heart)

Many procedural heart implementations suffer from "horns", self-intersecting loops, or flattened apex lobes because their control points do not maintain $C^1$ velocity continuity at the upper cleft and bottom cusp.

[`Heart`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/2d/Heart.ts) constructs two symmetric cubic Bézier curves joining the top cleft $P_0 = (0, -0.65h)$ to the bottom apex $P_3 = (0, 0.95h)$:

items: **Left Lobe**: Defined by control points $P_0, C_1, C_2, P_3$:

**Tangent Continuity**: At the bottom cusp $P_3$, the tangent vectors of both lobes share identical vertical inclinations $\frac{d\mathbf{B}_L}{dt}(1) \propto (w, -h)$ and $\frac{d\mathbf{B}_R}{dt}(1) \propto (-w, -h)$, producing a sharp, clean meeting point without loop artifacts.

blocks.text: 3.3. Compound Cutouts & Even-Odd Winding (Gear2D, Annulus)
In Retiam's analytical GPU vector shader, hollow shapes require multiple sub-paths with opposite winding directions:

items: **Outer Ring/Perimeter**: Counter-Clockwise (CCW) winding.
**Inner Cutout / Bore Hole**: Clockwise (CW) winding.

blocks.text: Involute Gear Profile (Gear2D)

[`Gear2D`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/2d/Gear2D.ts) computes $N$ mechanical teeth with addendum $r_{\text{tip}}$, dedendum $r_{\text{root}}$, and pressure angle $\phi$:

items: **Root Flank**: Arc at $r_{\text{root}}$ between adjacent teeth.
**Involute Drive Face**: Radial transition from $r_{\text{root}}$ to $r_{\text{tip}}$ inclined by angle $\delta = \frac{\pi}{2N}$.
**Tooth Tip**: Flat or filleted arc at $r_{\text{tip}}$.
**Coast Face**: Symmetric return to root circle.
**Center Bore & Keyway**: Appends a circular hole `M ... A ... A ... Z` with an optional rectangular keyway cutout $(w_{\text{key}} \times h_{\text{key}})$ for shaft mounting.

Tip (r_outer)
          ┌───┐
         /     \   <-- Involute Flanks
        /       \
  ─────┘         └───── Root (r_root)
        Teeth Cycle

blocks.text: 3.4. Lamé Superellipse Curves (Squircle)
A squircle is a special case of the Lamé curve defined by:

When $n = 2$, it yields a standard ellipse. When $n = 4$, it produces the canonical squircle. For any $n \ge 2$, [`Squircle`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/2d/Squircle.ts) evaluates parametric coordinates using sign-preserving fractional powers:
Sampled smoothly with $M = 128$ points and closed via an SVG polyline path.
4. 3D Procedural Mesh Generation & Analytical Shading
4.1. Flat Face Normals vs. Gouraud Spherical Banding (Platonic Solids)
In 3D mesh rendering, shared vertices with spherical normals produce severe shading artifacts on polyhedra:

When a flat polygon (e.g., a triangular face of a [`Tetrahedron`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/3d/PlatonicSolids.ts#L17) or a pentagonal face of a [`Dodecahedron`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/3d/PlatonicSolids.ts#L63)) shares vertices with adjacent faces, vertex normals point $109.5^\circ$ apart at the corners. When the GPU fragment shader linearly interpolates these normals, the flat facet renders as an **inflated spherical bubble**, creating curved specular blobs and dark perimeter halos:

blocks.code:
INCORRECT (Shared Radial Normals):
        n1 ↖        ↗ n2
            \      /
             ──────
             \    /   <-- GPU interpolates diverging normals
              \  /        Face appears curved like a bubble!
               \/
               n3 ↓

  CORRECT (Flat Face Normals):
        n ↑   n ↑   n ↑
        ───────────────   <-- Normal is constant across entire facet
             \    /           Uniform, crisp planar specular reflection!
              \  /
               \/

blocks.text: The Flat Shading Solution

[`generatePlatonicMesh`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/utils/meshGenerators.ts#L667) generates **distinct vertices per face**, calculating the exact outward-pointing unit normal of that plane:

items: **Tetrahedron**: 4 faces $\times$ 3 vertices = **12 vertices**, 4 triangles (12 indices).
**Octahedron**: 8 faces $\times$ 3 vertices = **24 vertices**, 8 triangles (24 indices).
**Icosahedron**: 20 faces $\times$ 3 vertices = **60 vertices**, 20 triangles (60 indices).
**Dodecahedron**: 12 pentagons $\times$ 5 vertices = **60 vertices**, 36 triangles (108 indices).

blocks.text: 4.2. Regular Dodecahedron Canonical Formulation
A regular dodecahedron has 20 vertices and 12 pentagonal faces. With golden ratio $\phi = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$ and inverse $\phi^{-1} = \frac{1}{\phi} = \phi - 1$:
The 12 planar, outward-oriented pentagons with uniform edge length $s = 2/\phi \approx 1.236$ are triangulated as:
Each pentagon $[v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4]$ is decomposed into three triangles: $(v_0, v_1, v_2)$, $(v_0, v_2, v_3)$, $(v_0, v_3, v_4)$.
4.3. Parallel Transport Bishop Frames (TorusKnot3D, Helix3D, Tube3D)
Standard Frenet-Serret frames fail when curve curvature vanishes ($\kappa(t) = 0$), causing the normal vector to flip $180^\circ$ and producing sudden mesh pinching.
[`generateTubeMesh`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/utils/meshGenerators.ts#L112) utilizes **Rotation-Minimizing (Bishop) Parallel Transport Frames**:
Given a smooth space curve $\mathbf{C}(t)$ with unit tangents $\mathbf{T}_i$:

items: **Initial Frame**: Choose an arbitrary normal $\mathbf{N}_0 \perp \mathbf{T}_0$, with binormal $\mathbf{B}_0 = \mathbf{T}_0 \times \mathbf{N}_0$.

**Parallel Transport**: For each subsequent point $i$, rotate the previous normal $\mathbf{N}_{i-1}$ around the axis of curvature $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{T}_{i-1} \times \mathbf{T}_i$ by angle $\alpha = \arccos(\mathbf{T}_{i-1} \cdot \mathbf{T}_i)$:

**Closed Loop Twist Equalization**: For closed curves (such as $(p, q)$ torus knots), any residual holonomy angle $\Delta\theta = \arccos(\mathbf{N}_0 \cdot \mathbf{N}_M)$ is distributed uniformly along the path:

blocks.text: This guarantees continuous cross-sections without pinching or localized twisting across complex knots.
4.4. Seamless Analytical Capsule (Capsule3D)
A 3D capsule consists of a cylindrical cylinder body joined to two hemispherical caps:

blocks.tex: \text{Top Cap: } y \in [h/2, h/2 + r], \quad \text{Cylinder: } y \in [-h/2, h/2], \quad \text{Bottom Cap: } y \in [-h/2 - r, -h/2]

blocks.text: [`generateCapsuleMesh`](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/libs/shapes/utils/meshGenerators.ts#L236) uses unified spherical coordinate rings spanning polar angle $\theta \in [0, \pi]$:

At the cylinder transition $\theta = \pi/2$, the cylindrical normal $(\cos\phi, 0, \sin\phi)$ is mathematically identical to the hemispherical normal, achieving **$C^1$ seamless normal continuity** across the weld line.
